chapter_summary:
As DevOps professionals, our goal extends beyond merely deploying code; we aim for seamless, low-risk deployments that minimize downtime and provide robust rollback capabilities. The "all-at-once" deployment, where all instances are updated simultaneously, is the simplest approach but carries the highest risk. If the new version has a critical bug, the entire application can become unavailable instantly, leading to significant customer impact and a frantic scramble to roll back. While suitable for non-critical internal applications or development environments, it's rarely acceptable for production workloads.

A significant improvement is the **rolling deployment** strategy. Instead of updating all instances at once, you update a small batch of instances, wait for them to pass health checks, and then proceed with the next batch. This process continues until all instances are running the new version. AWS Auto Scaling Groups (ASGs) inherently support rolling updates by terminating old instances and launching new ones with updated AMIs or launch configurations. For containerized applications, services like Amazon ECS and Kubernetes (EKS) also facilitate rolling updates by gradually replacing old containers with new ones. The primary benefit of rolling deployments is reduced downtime, as traffic can continue to be served by the healthy instances running the old version while updates occur. However, a key challenge is that for a period, both old and new versions of the application might be running simultaneously. This requires careful consideration of backward compatibility for APIs, database schemas, and data formats. If the new version introduces a breaking change, it could lead to errors for users hitting the "new" instances while other users are still interacting with "old" instances. Rollback in a rolling deployment involves initiating another rolling update to revert to the previous stable version, which can still take time and incur some service disruption.

To further mitigate risk and eliminate downtime, we turn to strategies like **blue/green deployments**. In a blue/green deployment, you maintain two identical, separate environments: "blue" (the currently active production environment) and "green" (the new environment where the updated application version is deployed and tested). Once the green environment is thoroughly validated, traffic is shifted from blue to green, typically using a load balancer or DNS change. AWS CodeDeploy, for instance, provides built-in support for blue/green deployments for EC2, ECS, and Lambda. The primary advantage here is zero downtime and instant rollback. If issues arise after the traffic shift, you can immediately revert traffic back to the original blue environment, which remains untouched and fully functional. This provides a safety net that drastically reduces the impact of failed deployments. The main drawback is the increased infrastructure cost, as you need to provision and maintain two full environments, even if one is idle for a period. Careful planning is also needed for stateful services like databases, as they cannot simply be duplicated; strategies like replication or shared databases with backward-compatible schema changes are essential.

The most cautious approach is the **canary deployment**. Inspired by the "canary in a coal mine" concept, a canary deployment involves releasing the new version to a very small subset of users or traffic (the "canary") while the majority of users continue to use the stable, old version. This allows you to monitor the performance and stability of the new version with real user traffic in a controlled manner. If the canary performs well and no errors are detected, the new version can be gradually rolled out to more users, eventually replacing the old version entirely. If issues are detected, the canary traffic can be immediately diverted back to the old version, limiting the blast radius of the problem to a tiny fraction of users. AWS services like Application Load Balancer (ALB) with weighted target groups, AWS App Mesh, and even AWS Lambda aliases can be used to implement canary deployments. Canary deployments offer the highest level of risk mitigation and are ideal for critical applications where even minor disruptions are unacceptable. The complexity, however, is significantly higher, requiring sophisticated monitoring, automated health checks, and often A/B testing frameworks to truly evaluate the new version's impact. It also requires a robust rollback mechanism to quickly revert the small percentage of traffic if issues are detected.

Regardless of the chosen strategy, the bedrock of successful advanced deployments is **automation** and **observability**. Automation, often implemented through CI/CD pipelines, ensures consistency, repeatability, and speed, reducing human error. Observability, encompassing comprehensive logging, metrics, and tracing, provides the critical feedback loop needed to detect issues quickly, understand their root cause, and validate the success of a deployment. Without these pillars, even the most sophisticated deployment strategy can fail to deliver its promised benefits. Understanding the nuances of each strategy and selecting the right one for a given application's criticality and risk tolerance is a hallmark of a professional DevOps engineer.

screens.title: Introduction to Advanced Deployment Strategies
screens.subtitle: Why deployment technique determines risk, downtime, and rollback capability

narration.text: In this chapter we’ll explore four advanced deployment strategies you will use as a professional DevOps engineer: all-at-once, rolling, blue/green, and canary. You will learn when each strategy reduces risk, what trade-offs it imposes on cost and complexity, and which AWS services commonly implement them. We’ll connect each approach to practical concerns: customer-facing downtime, the blast radius of failures, and the need for backward compatibility when multiple versions run concurrently. You’ll also see why automation and observability are not optional — they are the foundations that make safe rollouts possible. For example, a blue/green deployment gives you instant rollback at the cost of duplicated infrastructure, while a canary rollout reduces blast radius by serving a small percentage of real traffic to the new version. Throughout the chapter we’ll use concrete AWS examples such as Auto Scaling Groups, ECS/EKS, ALB weighted routing, Lambda aliases, and CodeDeploy so you can map strategy to platform. Notice the pattern: more safety requires more automation and more visibility. Consider this question as you begin: for a high-traffic, revenue-critical service, which trade-offs are you willing to accept?

keyIdea.title: Core message
keyIdea.text: Choose a deployment strategy that balances risk mitigation, downtime, and operational complexity; automation and observability are essential to make any strategy reliable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to differentiate the four advanced deployment strategies and select the right one for each risk profile. First, you will name and explain all-at-once, rolling, blue/green, and canary deployments and describe the fundamental trade-offs between risk, downtime, and operational complexity. Second, you will evaluate these strategies against application criticality and requirements for rollback speed, providing real examples of when each approach is appropriate. Third, you will map each strategy to AWS services such as Auto Scaling Groups, ECS/EKS, Application Load Balancer, Lambda aliases, and CodeDeploy, so you can design an implementation plan with concrete platform choices. Fourth, you will justify why automation and observability are mandatory: automation for repeatable rollouts and observability for detecting regressions and validating production health. Each objective focuses on applied understanding, not just definitions; you will practice conceptual scenarios and a hands-on simulation so you can show the difference in downtime and risk for yourself.

screens.title: All-at-once deployment
screens.subtitle: Definition, pros, cons, and when it is acceptable

narration.text: All-at-once deployment is the simplest approach: you update every instance or service simultaneously to the new version. As a definition, it means replacing the running environment wholesale with the new release in a single operation. A concrete example is stopping one EC2 instance running a container, rebuilding the image with a new version number, and starting that new image on the same instance — except done to every instance at the same time. The clear advantage is speed and minimal orchestration cost; you do not need complex orchestration or traffic routing to coordinate versions. The principal downside is risk: if the release contains a critical bug, the entire application becomes unavailable instantly. That exposes the business to a large blast radius and potentially long recovery while you roll back. A common misconception is that all-at-once is acceptable for production if you have fast rollback scripts. In reality, rollback scripts may reduce recovery time but cannot prevent customer-facing errors that occur between deploy and rollback. Acceptable use cases include internal tools, development environments, or very low-traffic services where brief downtime is tolerable. Key takeaway: simple but risky — reserve it for non-critical contexts and always combine it with strong automated tests and quick rollback procedures.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: All-at-once is fastest to execute but creates the largest blast radius; use only where downtime risk is acceptable.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › All-at-once
Definition

Update every instance simultaneously

You replace all running instances with the new release in a single operation. It requires minimal orchestration but carries high risk for production traffic.

Risk
Highest blast radius; entire service may go down if the release is faulty.
When to use
Internal tools, development environments, or low-criticality services where brief downtime is acceptable.
Concrete example
You have three EC2 instances behind a load balancer. An all-at-once deploy stops containers on all instances, updates images to version 2.0.0, and starts them. During the update window, no instance serves the old release, so users may see errors until all instances are healthy.
Key takeaway

Fast and simple, but not suitable for critical production services without compensation like exhaustive testing and very fast rollback automation.

screens.title: Rolling deployment
screens.subtitle: Batch updates, health checks, and backward compatibility concerns

narration.text: A rolling deployment updates the application in batches, replacing a small set of instances at a time. Conceptually you take a fraction of the fleet out of service, update it, validate health checks, and then proceed to the next batch until every instance runs the new version. AWS Auto Scaling Groups normally perform rolling style updates when you replace AMIs or change launch templates. Container orchestrators like Amazon ECS or Kubernetes also replace old containers incrementally. The major benefit is reduced downtime: traffic continues to be served by healthy instances while others are being updated. But this advantage introduces an important operational constraint: during the rollout both old and new versions coexist. That means backward compatibility becomes a first-class concern. For example, if you change an A P I payload format in the new version, some requests routed to new instances may fail when other services or clients still speak to old instances. A concrete mitigation is designing APIs to accept both old and new payloads or using feature flags to gate changes. Rollback in a rolling strategy is another rolling update, which reduces blast radius but can take time. A common misconception is that rolling eliminates risk — it reduces downtime but requires careful design around compatibility and testing. The key insight: rolling balances availability and risk but shifts emphasis to compatibility engineering and gradual verification.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Rolling updates reduce downtime but require backward compatibility and careful health checks while multiple versions coexist.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Rolling Deployment
Process

Update in batches with health gates

  1. 1. Take a small batch out of service.
  2. 2. Deploy new version to batch and run health checks.
  3. 3. If healthy, reattach and proceed; if not, halt and roll back.
AWS mappings: Auto Scaling Group rolling updates, ECS service rolling update, Kubernetes rolling update (EKS).
Example & concerns
With three instances, update one instance and verify health. While the other two serve traffic, some clients will hit the updated instance and require backward-compatible behavior. If you change database schema or API payloads, ensure compatibility or use feature flags to avoid errors.
Pro tip
Design API changes to accept old and new payloads for a transition period to avoid failures during the overlap window.
Common mistake
Assuming health checks alone guarantee compatibility; they confirm liveliness but not API contract correctness.

screens.title: Blue/Green deployment
screens.subtitle: Parallel environments, instant rollback, and state challenges

narration.text: Blue/green deployment uses two separate but identical environments: blue is the current production environment and green is the new environment where you deploy and validate the updated version. Once you are confident in the green environment you switch traffic from blue to green, typically by modifying a load balancer or DNS. The advantage is zero-downtime cutover and an instant rollback: if problems appear after switching, you simply shift traffic back to the untouched blue environment. AWS CodeDeploy supports blue/green for EC2, ECS, and Lambda, where the service helps manage traffic shifts and hooks for validation. The main drawback is cost: you operate two full environments in parallel which increases infrastructure expense. A deeper challenge is stateful services like databases. You cannot simply duplicate a stateful database without careful planning. Common strategies include replication, shared databases with backward-compatible schema changes, or feature toggles to manage data migrations. A typical misconception is that blue/green removes all risk; it reduces runtime deployment risk but introduces complexity in managing shared state and data migrations. The core engineering task is to design the environment and data strategy so that switching is safe and any rollback will not corrupt user data. Finally, plan health checks, integration tests, and a traffic-shift validation window before fully cutting over.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Blue/green provides instant rollback and zero downtime at the cost of duplicated infrastructure and careful state management.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Blue/Green
Architecture

Two parallel environments and a switch

Green environment is deployed and fully validated before traffic shifts. Rollback is a traffic switch back to blue.
AWS example: CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS or Lambda; use a load balancer or DNS change to shift traffic between environments.
Cost trade-off: maintaining two environments increases infrastructure spend while green is validated.
Stateful service concerns
Databases cannot simply be duplicated. Typical options are replication, carefully planned migrations with backward-compatible schema changes, or shared databases that accept both old and new schemas during transition.
Common mistake
Assuming environment parity equals data safety; always plan data migration and replication strategies before switching traffic.

screens.title: Canary deployment
screens.subtitle: Small-traffic rollouts, monitoring needs, and AWS implementations

narration.text: A canary deployment introduces the new version to a small subset of real user traffic — the canary — while the majority continues to use the stable version. The purpose is to monitor real-world behavior with a minimal blast radius. If metrics remain healthy, you increase the fraction of traffic until the new version fully replaces the old. Implementations in AWS include Application Load Balancer weighted target groups, AWS App Mesh for service-mesh routing, or Lambda aliases with weighted traffic. Canary deployments offer the highest risk mitigation because failures impact only a tiny user segment, but they come with increased complexity. You need sophisticated monitoring, automated health checks, and often A/B testing frameworks to interpret results. A concrete example: route 1% of traffic to version 2.0.0, monitor error rates and latency for that group, then move to 5%, 20%, and so on. A common misconception is that canary rollouts automatically reveal all issues; they only detect problems that appear under the sampled traffic and whose signals are observed by your metrics. Effective canaries require carefully chosen signals and automated gates so that progression pauses or reverts automatically on anomaly detection. The main engineering task is implementing the automation that increases traffic safely and the observability that decides when to stop or roll back.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Canary rollouts minimize blast radius through staged traffic increases but need advanced monitoring and automated gates to be safe.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Canary
Comparison

Stage traffic to a small subset and expand

Start with a tiny percentage of users, monitor, then gradually increase. AWS tools: ALB weighted routing, App Mesh, Lambda aliases.
Typical progression: 1% → 5% → 20% → 100% with automated health gates at each step.
Observability focus: error rate, latency distribution, and business metrics specific to the feature being released.
Example scenario
Route 1% of production traffic to the canary and monitor SLOs. If the canary’s error rate stays within acceptable thresholds, increase to 5%. If an anomaly appears, divert that traffic back to the stable release immediately.
Misconception
Assuming a canary will reveal every issue; some problems only appear at full scale or under specific user behaviors not present in the canary sample.

screens.title: Hands-on simulation: starter app and Docker
screens.subtitle: A simple Flask app and Dockerfile to practice deployment updates

narration.text: The chapter includes a simple Flask application and Dockerfile you can use to simulate updates and observe behavior. The app exposes a single route that returns its version number from an environment variable. This is a useful minimal example because you can change just the version string and observe routing, caching, or client behavior during different deployment strategies. The provided Dockerfile builds a small image and sets a default APP_VERSION environment variable so you can run distinct containers for 1.0.0 and 2.0.0. In practice, for an all-at-once update you would rebuild and redeploy the single instance and notice a service interruption window. For rolling updates you would update each instance image progressively. For blue/green you would build a green environment with the new image, validate it, and switch traffic. Pay attention to how the environment variable is set at container launch because this pattern lets you run multiple versions simultaneously on different hosts. Common traps include relying on local caches or DNS TTLs that delay traffic switching. When you later simulate a canary, you will route a small percentage of requests to containers running the new image and monitor logs and metrics. This starter app is intentionally simple so the deployment behavior is the learning focus.

keyIdea.title: Practice app
keyIdea.text: A simple versioned Flask app and Dockerfile let you experience downtime, compatibility, and routing differences across deployment strategies.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Starter App
Files
app.py
from flask import Flask
import os

app = Flask(__name__)

# Environment variable to define the version
APP_VERSION = os.environ.get('APP_VERSION', '1.0.0')

@app.route('/')
def hello_world():
  return f'Hello from Cohortia App! Version: {APP_VERSION}'

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=80)
Dockerfile
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
ENV APP_VERSION=1.0.0 # Default version
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
Instructions: build an image with a tag for each version and run containers with APP_VERSION set to the appropriate value to observe version behavior under different deployment strategies.

screens.title: Simulate all-at-once, rolling, and blue/green
screens.subtitle: Practical steps using EC2 and Docker to observe downtime and risk

narration.text: This exercise guides you through conceptual steps to simulate different deployment behaviors using a simple Dockerized web app on EC2. Start by launching an EC2 instance and installing Docker. Build and run the image for version 1.0.0 and verify the page shows the current version. For an all-at-once update on a single instance, stop the running container, build the image for version 2.0.0, and start the new container. Observe the service interruption while the container restarts and the container image loads; that is the downtime window. For a rolling update conceptualization imagine three EC2 instances behind a load balancer. Update one instance at a time: drain traffic from the instance, replace the container with version 2.0.0, wait for health checks to pass, and then reintroduce it. Ensure at least two instances continue serving traffic to reduce customer impact. For a blue/green conceptualization with two instances, provision an idle instance and deploy version 2.0.0 there. Validate it thoroughly, then change the load balancer target to point to the green instance. If issues appear, switch traffic back to blue immediately. In each scenario, take note of when both versions run concurrently, which exposes compatibility risks, and how long rollbacks would take. This hands-on framing helps you internalize the trade-offs between speed and safety.

keyIdea.title: Practice steps
keyIdea.text: Simulate the strategies on EC2 to observe downtime and compatibility issues: single-instance all-at-once, multi-instance rolling updates, and two-instance blue/green switches.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Simulation Steps
All-at-once (single EC2)
  • docker build -t my-app:2.0.0 .
  • docker stop my-app-v1 && docker run -d -p 80:80 --name my-app-v2 -e APP_VERSION=2.0.0 my-app:2.0.0
  • Observe downtime while container restarts.
Rolling (three instances)
  • Remove one instance from rotation, update container, wait for health checks.
  • Return instance to rotation; repeat for next instance.
  • Ensure compatibility since old and new versions coexist briefly.
Blue/Green (two instances)
  • Deploy v2.0.0 to idle green instance and run integration tests.
  • Switch load balancer target from blue to green; validate traffic.
  • If issues, switch back to blue for instant rollback.
Note: these steps are conceptual instructions to help you design and observe rollout behaviors; adapt commands to your environment and security rules.

screens.title: Automation and Observability
screens.subtitle: Why pipelines and signals make advanced deployments safe

narration.text: Automation and observability are the two pillars that enable safe advanced deployments. Automation — typically implemented in CI/CD pipelines — makes rollouts repeatable, removes manual error-prone steps, and provides hooks for automated rollbacks. Observability supplies the feedback loop: logs, metrics, and traces tell you if the new version behaves correctly under real load. A concrete example is an automated pipeline that deploys a canary, runs synthetic tests, and evaluates error-rate and latency metrics before promoting the release. If the metric thresholds are breached, the pipeline automatically re-routes traffic or runs a rollback. Observability must be designed to capture both system-level signals (C P U, error rate, latency) and business-level signals (conversion rate, checkout errors) so you can judge production impact. A common misconception is treating health checks alone as sufficient observability; health checks indicate basic liveness but not business correctness or performance regressions. Another trap is insufficient alerting configuration that produces either no signal or noise. The engineering task is to tie automated gates to meaningful signals and to test rollback paths routinely. In short, the safest strategy is only as good as your ability to automate its execution and to observe its effects in production in real time.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Automation makes rollouts repeatable; observability tells you whether a rollout succeeded. Both are required to reduce risk reliably.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Automation & Observability
Automation
Pipelines and automated gates
  • CI/CD pipelines enforce repeatable deployment steps and provide rollback hooks.
  • Automated gates evaluate observability signals before proceeding to the next stage.
  • Test rollback paths regularly to ensure fast recovery when needed.
Observability
Logs, metrics, and traces that matter
  • System metrics: error rate, latency, resource utilization.
  • Business metrics: transaction success rate, checkout conversions.
  • Synthetic checks and distributed traces to narrow root causes quickly.
Pro tip: connect your pipeline to observability so promotion occurs automatically only when signals are within gate thresholds.

screens.title: Evaluating trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Risk, downtime, complexity, and cost across strategies

narration.text: Choosing a deployment strategy is an act of trade-off analysis. Use the deployment’s business criticality to weigh risk versus cost and complexity. All-at-once maximizes speed but also maximizes blast radius and user-facing downtime. Rolling reduces downtime but requires compatibility engineering because versions overlap. Blue/green offers zero downtime and instant rollback at the cost of duplicated infrastructure and careful data management. Canary provides the smallest blast radius and the most controlled validation, but it requires sophisticated monitoring and automated traffic management. A concrete evaluation example: for a mission-critical e-commerce checkout microservice you will likely prioritize zero downtime and minimal blast radius, steering you to blue/green or canary with heavy observability. A low-traffic internal analytics job might tolerate all-at-once to save cost. Complexity also matters: canary rollouts require weighted routing or service-mesh configuration, plus automated gates, which increases operational overhead. A common pitfall is prioritizing infrastructure cost over user risk without quantifying the potential revenue or reputation loss from outages. Always include rollback time, testing coverage, and observability maturity in your evaluation. The mature decision ties the deployment strategy to business SLOs and the team’s ability to operate the chosen approach reliably.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Match strategy to business criticality: more critical services justify higher complexity and cost to minimize blast radius and downtime.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Trade-offs
All-at-once
Fast, low complexity, highest risk, low cost.
Rolling
Lower downtime, compatibility required, moderate complexity.
Blue/Green
Zero downtime, instant rollback, higher infrastructure cost.
Canary
Minimized blast radius, highest monitoring needs, greatest complexity.
Decision rule
Prioritize minimizing blast radius and rollback speed for high criticality systems; accept higher cost and complexity when business impact is large.

screens.title: Design checklist for safe rollouts
screens.subtitle: Compatibility, testing, gating, rollback, and observability

narration.text: Before you choose and run a deployment, follow a checklist that ties engineering practices to the chosen strategy. Start with compatibility: ensure A P I changes are backward-compatible or provide adapters and feature flags so old and new versions coexist safely. Next, expand test coverage with integration and canary-targeted tests that exercise the new behaviors under representative traffic. Third, wire automated gates into your CI/CD pipeline that evaluate observability signals such as error rate, latency percentiles, and business metrics before promoting a rollout. Fourth, prepare rollback artifacts and scripts so you can revert quickly — in blue/green that means switching traffic, for rolling it means a reverse rolling update, and for canary it means diverting canary traffic away. Fifth, validate your monitoring: ensure traces and logs are sampled for the new version and that dashboards can compare old and new performance. A common mistake is leaving rollback paths untested; a rollback that fails or corrupts data can be worse than the original problem. Finally, run tabletop exercises or rehearsals to validate the entire process. This checklist connects the abstract strategy to concrete steps you can verify, which is essential for operating critical services safely.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use a pre-deployment checklist focused on compatibility, testing, automated gates, rollback readiness, and observability validation.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Design Checklist
Compatibility
Ensure APIs and schemas accept both old and new formats or use feature flags.
Testing
Add integration and canary-targeted tests that run as part of the pipeline.
Automated gates
Tie progression to meaningful metrics with automatic halt/rollback on anomalies.
Rollback readiness
Prepare scripts and test the rollback path regularly to ensure fast recovery.
Observability
Capture system and business metrics, traces, and logs for both old and new versions.
Rehearsal
Run tabletop exercises and dry-run deployments to validate procedures and timing.
Key Takeaway: checklists convert strategy into reliable operational steps your team can execute under pressure.

screens.title: Rollback strategies and blast radius
screens.subtitle: How rollback choice affects recovery and impact scope

narration.text: Rollback planning should be part of your deployment design from the start. The rollback mechanism you choose determines how quickly you can recover and how large the blast radius of a failed release becomes. In blue/green, rollback is the simplest operationally: redirect traffic back to the untouched blue environment and continue investigation. In canary deployments, rollback often means diverting the small percentage of traffic away from the canary, which contains the issue to a few users. In rolling updates, rollback entails another rolling operation to restore the previous version, which can be time-consuming and may still expose users during the rollback window. All-at-once relies on redeploying the previous version or restoring a snapshot, but the downtime impact is high. A concrete scenario: a new release introduces an error in payment processing. With blue/green you cut back to blue immediately and payments resume; with rolling you may have to update multiple instances before stability returns, causing longer customer impact. A frequent misconception is that rollback is just a manual switch; in production you must automate rollback triggers based on observability gates so human response time does not enlarge the blast radius. The key insight: faster and safer rollback patterns reduce both business impact and operational stress during incidents.

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Design rollback for speed and safety: automation and small blast radii make recovery less disruptive and faster.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.1 › Rollback & Blast Radius
Rollback patterns
  • Blue/green: traffic switch back to blue for instant rollback.
  • Canary: divert canary traffic away to limit impact to a small group.
  • Rolling: reverse the rolling update, which takes time and coordination.
  • All-at-once: redeploy previous version or restore from snapshot; downtime likely.
Blast radius
Blast radius is the scope of impact from a failed release. Smaller blast radii reduce customer exposure and simplify incident response. Canary and well-configured blue/green approaches minimize blast radius when implemented with automation.
Pro tip: automate rollback triggers on critical observability signals to limit the human reaction time that otherwise expands blast radius.

narration.text: Here are three central concepts to hold on to. First, all-at-once deploys everything at once — it's quick but exposes the entire service to any bug introduced by the release. Second, rolling deployments update instances in batches, which reduces downtime but requires backward compatibility because old and new versions coexist. Third, blue/green maintains two environments and switches traffic to achieve zero downtime and instant rollback, with a cost trade-off and careful attention to state and data migration. Each concept trades off risk, downtime, and complexity differently, and understanding these trade-offs is the foundation of choosing a strategy that fits your service’s tolerance for disruption.
